text: For decades, enterprise security worked like a castle with a moat: build a strong wall around everything, control the few gates in and out, and trust whatever makes it inside. Zero Trust throws that model out. Its core principle is blunt — never grant trust based on network location alone. Every request gets verified explicitly, every time, no matter where it comes from.

Under the old model, a password-protected Wi-Fi network or a VPN connection was often the whole security check — once inside, traffic ran with minimal scrutiny. Zero Trust replaces that single perimeter check with a check on every single request. Location isn't ignored, but by itself it's never a reason to skip verification; who's asking and what they're asking for matter far more than where they're asking from.

Most real-world Zero Trust frameworks rest on three tenets. Verify explicitly: authenticate and authorize using every available signal, every time. Least privilege access: grant only the access actually needed, for only as long as it's needed. Assume breach: design and monitor as if an attacker is already inside, so a single compromise can't spread far.

Two things broke the old model at once. Remote work meant employees started connecting from home networks and coffee shops with no relationship to the corporate perimeter. Cloud adoption meant the apps and data they needed had already moved outside that perimeter too, sitting in Azure or AWS and reachable over the open internet by design. With both users and resources outside the walls, there was no single boundary left to defend, and no meaningful line left between trusted and untrusted based on location alone.

That's the whole shift in one sentence: trust used to come from being inside the network, and now it has to be earned on every request, from every identity, every time. Next up: how that principle gets applied directly to network design, breaking one large trusted zone into many small, tightly secured segments.
